1.why: The UI uses a clean sans-serif typeface with clear letter spacing and comfortable line height across all screens.

2.why: Instructions use sentence case with no italics, all-caps, or dense paragraphs; text is broken into short lines and callout boxes.

3.why: Layouts are single-column, narrow, and fully readable in the mobile-width screenshots with adequately sized controls.

4.why: All instructional copy is brief and uses plain wording such as “Enter the six-digit code” and “Keep these codes somewhere safe.”

5.why: Placeholders show expected formats (e.g., “Six digits”, “ABCDE-23456”) and the demo-account callout gives a concrete example, though not every field has a live sample.

6.why: No screen requires reading a long block; each step presents only a short sentence or two plus a single callout.

7.why: The manual secret and recovery codes are rendered as ordinary selectable text that can be copied, although no explicit “Copy” button is provided.

8.why: No QR code or equivalent scannable alternative appears; the flow explicitly tells the user to add the secret manually.

9.why: Standard email, tel and password inputs are used on the login form, which browsers and password managers can autofill; OTP fields remain plain text inputs.

10.why: A “Step X of 5” badge and a prominent filled blue primary button make the current step and main action visually obvious on every screen.

11.why: Each screen presents essentially one primary action (Continue, Verify identity, Generate, Confirm, Save codes, etc.).

12.why: Success banners such as “You have been logged out” and “Recovery code accepted and consumed” state what happened, though “what comes next” is sometimes left implicit by the step change.

13.why: Users can regenerate recovery codes, retry login after errors, and re-enter codes; the only constraint is a five-minute setup expiry noted on the authenticator screen.

14.why: The observed error (“We could not complete that request. Please try again.”) names the failure and suggests a fix without blaming the user, though it is generic.

15.why: A five-minute expiry is explicitly imposed on authenticator setup, so a time limit exists even though ordinary reading is untimed.
